title: Kaulajñānanirṇaya
summary: A dialogue of Bhairava and the Goddess in twenty-four chapters, 'brought down' by Macchaghnapāda (Matsyendra) from Candradvīpa as the Yoginīkaula. It teaches creation and dissolution within the body, the body-liṅga worshipped with inner flowers, the eleven centres of the body, nectar-meditations that conquer death and old age, the Kula and Akula, the eight-by-eight yoginīs, the qualifications of disciple, Śakti and hero, Kaula rites, and the story of how Bhairava as a fisherman recovered the scripture from a fish's belly.

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Bhairava to the Goddess; brought down (avatārita) by Śrī Macchaghnapāda / Mīnapāda / Matsyendrapāda from Candradvīpa (chapter colophons).
attribution.scholarly: Attributed to Matsyendra's school; edited from a Nepalese manuscript which the editor dated by its script to about the 11th century.

scholarly.text: c. 9th–11th c. (manuscript c. 11th c. per its editor)

structure.description: 24 paṭalas and a short concluding passage (ed. Bagchi); Bhairava–Devī dialogue

editions.name: P. C. Bagchi (ed.), Kaulajñānanirṇaya and some minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 3 (Calcutta, 1934)
Muktabodha e-text M00027 (from Bagchi 1934)
English translation by Michael Magee (Varanasi: Prachya Prakashan, 1986)

notes: U21 owns this source entry (U24 references it). The Magee translation is recalled, not checked.

title: Akulavīratantra
summary: A short tantra in two recensions praising the Akulavīra — the one reality beyond all distinctions, the same in everything, beyond mind, caste, ritual, fasting and pilgrimage. It teaches that the self is god, goddess, disciple and guru, that powers and alchemy are not to be grasped, and that the Kaula path is of two kinds, 'made' (kṛtaka: the aroused kuṇḍalī) and 'innate' (sahaja: abiding in samarasa).

attribution.tradition: Brought down by Macchendrapāda, obtained by the grace of the yoginī at Kāmarūpa (colophon).
attribution.scholarly: Matsyendra school; edited by Bagchi from Nepalese manuscripts in two recensions (A and B).

structure.description: two recensions: A (51 verses before a lacuna of pp. 89–96 in the edition) and B (continuing from v. 39 after the lacuna to c. 130+ verses)

editions.name: P. C. Bagchi (ed.), Kaulajñānanirṇaya and some minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 3 (Calcutta, 1934)
Muktabodha e-text M00003

notes: Refs in this shard use 'A.n' for the first recension and 'B.n' for the text after the lacuna in the e-text; the assignment of the post-lacuna verses to recension B follows the e-text's layout and should be checked against the printed edition.

title: Kulānandatantra
summary: A brief Bhairava–Devī dialogue on centres in the body (the sixty-four-petalled lotus in the brahma-place and others) and the quickly convincing signs of Kaula practice: bewitching, piercing, shaking, trembling, moving in the sky, samarasa and the removal of wrinkles and grey hair.

editions.name: P. C. Bagchi (ed.), Kaulajñānanirṇaya and some minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 3 (Calcutta, 1934)
Muktabodha e-text M00513

title: Jñānakārikā
summary: A short work in three chapters — on liberation (mokṣādhikāra), on dharma and adharma, and on conduct (caryā) — teaching that bondage is support (āśraya) and liberation is supportlessness, that dharma and adharma are two nooses to be cut with the sword of knowledge, and that the 'fourth' mind beyond the three guṇas is marked by nirvāṇa.

editions.name: P. C. Bagchi (ed.), Kaulajñānanirṇaya and some minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 3 (Calcutta, 1934)
Muktabodha e-text M00024

title: Yogaviṣaya
summary: A short tract of thirty-three verses attributed to Mīnanātha (Matsyendra): the qualified disciple, the six centres from ādhāra to ājñā, the three channels, the three knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, the names of kuṇḍalinī, the nectar raining from the brahma-place, inner worship with the flower of the mind, and the haṃsa repeated 21,600 times as 'so 'ham'.

editions.name: P. C. Bagchi (ed.), Kaulajñānanirṇaya and some minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 3 (Calcutta, 1934)
Muktabodha e-text M00121

notes: Colophon in the e-text reads 'matsyendranāthaviracitaṃ ...'; the text calls its author Mīnanātha, son of Umā and Śaṅkara (v. 7). Date uncertain.

title: Candrāvalokana
summary: A short dialogue in which Maheśvara instructs Matsyendra on the śāmbhavī seal (inner aim, outer unwinking gaze), the dissolution of breath and mind, the 'new-moon, first-day and full-moon' of the eyes, desire (kāma), poison (viṣa) and the spotless (nirañjana), the mind as the seed from which bindu arises, and the six centres.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00506 ('Candrāvalocakana')

notes: Several verses are shared with the Haṭhapradīpikā (e.g. the verse ending 'dambha-mithyā-pralāpaḥ' = HYP 4.114). Date unknown.

title: Matsyendrasaṃhitā
summary: A Śaiva tantric compendium on yoga and ritual transmitted in Matsyendra's name, teaching the body's centres and channels, kuṇḍalinī, khecarī and related practices within a Kaula/Śākta frame.
notes: Recalled: a partial critical edition exists (C. Kiss, Oxford DPhil); chapter count and contents to be checked in sourcing. Not available locally.

title: Gorakṣaśataka
summary: 'The hundred of Gorakṣa': a short haṭha manual of six-limbed yoga (posture, breath-control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation, samādhi). It teaches siddhāsana and padmāsana, the centres, ten channels and ten breaths, the awakening of kuṇḍalinī, five seals and locks, the sun and moon and the reversed practice, the five element-concentrations, meditation with and without qualities, and samādhi as the one taste of breath and mind.

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Gorakṣa for the release from the noose of existence (v. 1).
attribution.scholarly: Several different texts carry this title. The text printed by Kuvalayananda and Shukla (and, in a longer form, by Nowotny) is identified by scholars as a recension of the Vivekamārtaṇḍa family; the 'original Gorakṣaśataka' is a different text (src:goraksasataka-mallinson).

structure.description: 101 verses in the Kuvalayananda–Shukla edition (GRETIL numbering, vv. 81 and 95 not numbered in the e-text)

editions.name: Gorakṣaśataka, ed. Swami Kuvalayananda and S. A. Shukla (Lonavla: Kaivalyadhama); GRETIL e-text

notes: Refs in this shard follow the Kuvalayananda–Shukla (GRETIL) numbering. U28 may add the haṭha analysis.

title: Gorakṣaśataka (recension printed by Briggs)
summary: The Gorakṣaśataka in the recension printed by G. W. Briggs (1938) and found as the first hundred verses of the Gorakṣapaddhati: after praising Mīnanātha it teaches the six limbs, the two postures, the knowledge of the six centres, sixteen supports, three aims and five voids of one's own body, the channels and breaths, and ends with the purification of the channels by alternate breathing.

structure.description: 101 verses (Muktabodha e-text M00522); numbering runs about three verses ahead of the Kuvalayananda–Shukla text at the start

editions.name: Gorakṣaśataka (the recension printed by Briggs, 1938); Muktabodha e-text M00522
G. W. Briggs, Gorakhnāth and the Kānphaṭa Yogīs (Calcutta, 1938)

title: Gorakṣaśataka (the 'original' Gorakṣaśataka)
summary: A distinct text transmitted under the same title, identified and translated by J. Mallinson as the original Gorakṣaśataka: a manual of about a hundred verses teaching yoga through the control of the breath, the stirring of Sarasvatī (sarasvatīcālana), several kinds of breath retention and the three locks; several of its verses reappear in the Haṭhapradīpikā.

editions.name: J. Mallinson, 'The Original Gorakṣaśataka', in D. G. White (ed.), Yoga in Practice (Princeton, 2012)

notes: Id disambiguated by editor per the data model. Contents recalled in outline only; not available locally.

title: Gorakṣapaddhati
summary: A compilation in two śatakas ascribed to Gorakṣa, the first corresponding to the Gorakṣaśataka in Briggs's recension and the second continuing with breath-control, the five concentrations, meditation and samādhi.

editions.name: printed with a Hindi commentary (Bombay: Khemraj Shrikrishnadas; editor recalled as Mahīdhara Śarmā — to be checked)

title: Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati
summary: The principal doctrinal treatise of the Nāth tradition, ascribed to Gorakṣanātha, in six upadeśas: the origin of the body (piṇḍotpatti) from the Supreme through its own power; the knowledge of the body (nine centres, sixteen supports, three aims, five voids); the vision of the cosmos in the body (piṇḍa-saṃvitti); the support of the body (Śakti); the samarasa of the body with the supreme state (pada); and the marks of the avadhūta yogī.

attribution.scholarly: Ascribed to Gorakṣa; some manuscripts are associated with Nityanātha; date uncertain and later than the earliest haṭha texts.

editions.name: K. Mallik (ed.), Siddha-siddhānta-paddhati and other works of the Nātha Yogīs (Poona, 1954)
M. L. Gharote and G. K. Pai (Lonavla: Lonavla Yoga Institute, 2005)

notes: Not available locally; teachings in this shard are given at upadeśa level with low/moderate confidence. The Nityanātha attribution is recalled, not checked.

title: Amaraughaprabodha
summary: A short work ascribed to Gorakṣanātha on the four yogas — mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja — in which haṭha practices (the great seal, great lock and great piercing) serve rājayoga, the goal; it describes the stages of practice and the sounds heard in them. Several of its verses reappear in the Haṭhapradīpikā.

editions.name: printed in K. Mallik (ed.), Siddha-siddhānta-paddhati and other works of the Nātha Yogīs (Poona, 1954) — to be checked

notes: U21 owns the source entry (registry). Distinct from the Kashmiri prose Amaraughaśāsana (src:amaraughasasana). Contents recalled in outline; not available locally.

title: Amaraughaśāsana
summary: A prose treatise ascribed to Gorakṣanātha, printed in the Kashmir Series with a commentary. It sets out the elements, breaths, channels, ten doors and seven bonds of the body, locates the 'desire, poison and spotless' (kāma, viṣa, nirañjana) at the root of the brahma-staff, rejects rival definitions of liberation (cutting off karma, Veda-recitation, the supportless, meditation on form, bindu and nāda, Kaula union, the movement of kuṇḍalinī) and defines liberation as the mind seeing the mind in sahaja-samādhi.

structure.description: 80 numbered prose sections (GRETIL numbering) with a verse commentary

editions.name: Amaraughaśāsana, ed. Mukund Ram Shastri, KSTS 20 (Bombay: Nirnaya-Sagara, 1918); GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig)

title: Gorakṣasaṃhitā
summary: Name of more than one text ascribed to Gorakṣa; among them a work on Kaula and yogic matters printed in the 20th century. Contents not recalled with confidence.
notes: Listed from the unit brief; kept as a stub with low confidence. Which text(s) carry this title must be established in sourcing (listed as a gap).

title: Yogamārtaṇḍa
summary: A haṭha text ascribed to Gorakṣa, closely related to the Gorakṣaśataka/Vivekamārtaṇḍa family of texts.
notes: Relation to src:vivekamartanda (U28) to be established; possibly an alternate title of a member of the same family. Low confidence.

title: Gorakṣasiddhāntasaṅgraha
summary: A late compilation of quotations setting out Nāth doctrine (the avadhūta, the origin of the body, the Nāth lineage and its superiority to other paths), drawing on the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati and tantras.

editions.name: ed. Gopinath Kaviraj, Princess of Wales Sarasvati Bhavana Texts (Benares, 1925)

title: Siddhasiddhāntasaṅgraha
summary: A verse summary of the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati ascribed to Balabhadra.

editions.name: ed. Gopinath Kaviraj (Benares, 1925) — to be checked

title: Gorakṣaguṭikā
summary: A tract framed as a Śiva–Gaurī dialogue said to belong to the Kalpadrumavivekinī: a first chapter on the birth and deeds of Gorakṣa (with its own account of his origin and ear-splitting) followed by liturgical hymns to Gorakṣanātha — twelve names, armour (kavaca), heart, five-jewel praise, 108 and 1000 names.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00291

notes: Shows the Nāth liturgy of guru-worship; its origin story differs from the better-known vernacular accounts.

title: Gorakṣayogaśāstra (Mūlasāra)
summary: A short stotra-like work ascribed to Gorakṣa listing the contents of the subtle body — channels, sun, moon and fire, centres and Kaula seats, the fourteen worlds, oceans and rivers within the body, and the moon on the inner Meru raining nectar — to be recited daily.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00288

title: Gorakṣamudgara
summary: An ornate poem ascribed to Gorakṣa, of which the first chapter ('destruction of ignorance and delusion') survives: it praises the one who realises his own nature within his body and preaches renunciation through seeing the transience of life and attachment.

editions.name: Muktabodha e-text M00289 (first pariccheda only)

title: Gorakh Bānī
summary: The Hindi (old Hindi / Sadhukkaḍī) sayings ascribed to Gorakhnāth: sabadīs (couplet-sayings), pads (songs) and short works such as the Machhīndra Gorakh Bodh, Ātma Bodh, Narvai Bodh, Abhai Mātrā Jog, Sisṭ Purāṇ, Pandrah Tithi, Sapt Vār and Romāvalī. They teach the yogī's restraint and middle way, the guru, the unstruck sound, the sky-circle and its inverted well of nectar, the retention of bindu, the conquest of death by 'dying the death Gorakh died', and the rejection of temple, mosque and caste.

attribution.scholarly: A body of sayings in early Hindi ascribed to Gorakh, collected from manuscripts by Baṛthvāl; the language points to c. 14th–16th c. transmission.

editions.name: Pītāmbaradatta Baṛthvāl (ed.), Gorakh-bānī (Prayag: Hindi Sahitya Sammelan, 1942)

notes: Registry id. Not available locally; sabadī numbers not recalled, so teachings use section-level refs.

title: Machhīndra Gorakh Bodh
summary: A question-and-answer dialogue in the Gorakh Bānī in which Gorakh asks and Matsyendra answers on the yogī's life: where the mind dwells, how to walk, sit and speak, and how the breath, the sky and the void are known.

title: Nāth Siddhoṁ kī Bāniyāṁ
summary: A collection of Hindi sayings of Nāth siddhas other than Gorakh — Carpaṭ, Cauraṅgī, Bharthari, Gopīcand, Jālandharī-pāv and others — edited by Hazārīprasād Dvivedī.

editions.name: ed. Hazārīprasād Dvivedī (Kashi: Nagari Pracharini Sabha, 1957)

title: Prāṇ Saṅkalī
summary: A short Hindi work ascribed to Cauraṅgīnāth, in which the speaker tells his own story (a prince maimed at a stepmother's accusation and restored by the Nāth gurus) and teaches breath and yoga.
notes: Attribution and contents recalled with low confidence; to be checked in sourcing.

title: Kabīr–Gorakh Goṣṭhī
summary: A dialogue text of the Kabīr Panth staging a debate between Kabīr and Gorakhnāth, in which Kabīr's devotion to the Name and the inner guru is shown as surpassing the yogī's practices.
notes: A sectarian composition; the meeting is chronologically impossible on scholarly dates. Recorded as the opponent's portrayal of the Nāth side (see dsp:kabir-and-the-yogis).

title: Gorakṣavijaya
summary: A Bengali narrative poem of the Nāth cycle telling how Gorakṣa, disguised as a dancer and drummer, awakens his guru Mīnanātha, who had forgotten himself among the women of the Kadalī kingdom, and brings him back to yoga.

title: Mīnacetana
summary: 'The awakening of Mīna': a Bengali version of the story of Gorakṣa rescuing Mīnanātha from the Kadalī kingdom.

title: Mānikcandra Rājār Gān
summary: A North Bengal ballad of Queen Mayanāmatī, disciple of Gorakṣa, and her son King Gopīcandra, whom she makes renounce the kingdom and take initiation from Hāḍipā (Jālandhara) to escape early death.

editions.name: G. A. Grierson, 'The Song of Mānik Candra', Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1878)

title: Gopīcandrer Sannyās
summary: A Bengali poem of the Gopīcandra cycle on the king's renunciation under Hāḍipā at his mother Mayanāmatī's urging.
notes: Author recalled as Śukur Mahammad (uncertain); left out of 'authors' until sourced.

title: Gopīcand and Bharthari sagas (oral)
summary: Oral epics sung by householder Nāth jogīs in Rajasthan and the Hindi belt about King Gopīcand's renunciation and King Bharthari (Bhartṛhari) of Ujjain, who renounced after the episode of the fruit of immortality and became Gorakh's disciple.

title: Navanātha Bhaktisāra
summary: A Marathi verse narrative of the nine Nāths — Macchindra, Gorakh, Jālandhar, Kānif, Carpaṭ, Nāg, Bhartarī, Revaṇ and Gahinī — presented as incarnations of the nine Nārāyaṇas (the nine Yogendras of the Bhāgavata), with Dattātreya as their teacher.

tradition.text: composed Śaka 1741 (1819 CE) as generally stated

notes: Author recalled as Dhuṇḍisuta Mālu (Narahari Mālu); year recalled, not checked.

title: Navanāthacaritramu
summary: A Telugu narrative poem by Gauraṇa on the Nāth siddhas, including the story of Sāraṅgadhara (identified with Cauraṅgī), maimed at a stepmother's false accusation and restored by Matsyendra.

title: Qissa Pūran Bhagat
summary: Punjabi verse romance of Pūraṇ Bhagat, son of Rājā Salvāhan of Sialkot, maimed at his stepmother Lūṇā's false accusation, restored by Gorakhnāth and made a yogī — identified in Nāth tradition with Cauraṅgīnāth.
notes: Best-known version by Qādaryār (19th c., recalled). Context for the Cauraṅgī legend.

title: Hīr (Wāris Shāh)
summary: Wāris Shāh's Punjabi romance (1766) of Hīr and Rāñjhā; Rāñjhā goes to Tilla Jogian, takes the split-ear initiation from Bālnāth and wanders as a jogī — a detailed outsider's depiction of Nāth initiation and discipline.
notes: Sufi-context literature, used as context only for the depiction of Nāth practice.

title: Padmāvat
summary: Malik Muhammad Jāyasī's Avadhi epic (1540), in which King Ratansen takes the yogī's guise — earrings, patched cloak, horn and begging bowl — to seek Padmāvatī; context for the Nāth insignia in the 16th century.
notes: Sufi-context literature, context only.

title: Varṇaratnākara
summary: Jyotirīśvara's early Maithili prose encyclopedia of descriptions, which includes a list of eighty-four siddhas mixing names known from Nāth and Buddhist lists (Mīnanātha, Gorakṣanātha, Cauraṅgī and others).
notes: U49 may treat the siddha-list overlap in detail.

title: Vivekasār
summary: Bābā Kīnārām's principal Hindi work on discrimination (vivek) and Aghora yoga: the nature of the self and the supreme, the body as the dwelling of the supreme, the guru and the state beyond mind.

tradition.text: 18th c. (the tradition connects it with Kīnārām's vision of Dattātreya at Girnar)

notes: Coverage-map item. Contents known only in outline; no verse-anchored teachings created (gap).

title: Rāmgītā (Kīnārām)
summary: A Hindi work of Kīnārām teaching Rām as the attributeless supreme.

title: Rāmrasāl
summary: A devotional Hindi work of Kīnārām on Rām.

title: Gītāvalī (Kīnārām)
summary: A collection of Kīnārām's songs.

title: Unmunīrām
summary: A short work ascribed to Kīnārām on the unmanī state ('Rām of the unmanī').
notes: Title recalled with low confidence.
